questions.question: Explain why a school building with a raised floor needs both a flight of stairs and a wheelchair ramp.
questions.expected_answer: Stairs move many people quickly in a small space but exclude wheelchair users, people with prams or trolleys, learners on crutches and many older people. A ramp gives access to everyone but is long and slow because it must be gentle. Public buildings including schools must be accessible by law, so the ramp is required, and the stairs are kept for speed and throughput. Together they serve all users and give two routes.

questions.question: A classroom floor is 600 millimetres above the playground. Work out a suitable number of steps and the length of a ramp at 1 in 12, and explain what each number means for the user.
questions.expected_answer: With a riser of 150 millimetres, 600 divided by 150 gives four equal steps; equal risers of 150 to 180 millimetres match a comfortable stride and prevent trips. A gradient of 1 in 12 means one unit up for every twelve along, so 600 millimetres of rise needs 12 times 600, which is 7 200 millimetres of ramp; this gentle slope matches the force a wheelchair user can push with their arms. Treads of at least 250 millimetres fit a whole foot, and widths of about 1 200 millimetres let people pass.

questions.question: State the requirements for handrails and landings on the stairs and ramp, and give the reason behind each.
questions.expected_answer: Handrails on both sides at 900 to 1 000 millimetres above the surface, extending beyond the top and bottom, because that is hand height for a standing adult and a person needs to grip before the first step; a lower rail at about 700 millimetres and a kerb along the ramp help wheelchair users. Level landings at least 1 200 millimetres long at the top and bottom, at every change of direction and every 10 metres of ramp, so that users can rest their arms and open the door from a flat surface clear of the door swing. Surfaces must be non-slip for rain.
